North America. The northern continent of the Americas, encompassing the United States, Canada, Mexico, and numerous Caribbean island nations, stretching from the Arctic Ocean to the tropical region of Central America.

Bounded by the Atlantic Ocean to the east, the Pacific Ocean to the west, and the Arctic Ocean to the north, North America merges with Central America and the Caribbean to the south. It encompasses vast mountain ranges, great plains, deserts, and ancient forests.

The Mississippi River, one of the world's longest rivers, drains much of central North America and was crucial to Indigenous trade networks and later European-American expansion and commerce.

Indigenous peoples inhabited North America for at least fifteen thousand years before European contact, developing diverse civilizations from the Ancestral Puebloans of the Southwest to the Haudenosaunee Confederacy in the Northeast, with sophisticated governance, agriculture, and trade systems.

European colonization intensified in the sixteenth to eighteenth centuries with Spanish, French, English, and Dutch expeditions. Competition among these powers for colonial control shaped North American political boundaries and international conflicts.

The United States declared independence from Britain in seventeen seventy-six and established itself as a republic. Its westward expansion, codified in the concept of Manifest Destiny, displaced Indigenous peoples and extended territorial control to the Pacific Ocean.

Canada emerged as a British dominion in eighteen sixty-seven, gradually acquiring sovereignty. It represents a different colonial trajectory—less revolutionary than the United States and maintaining stronger ties to Britain and the Commonwealth.

The American Civil War from eighteen sixty-one to eighteen sixty-five determined that the United States would remain a unified nation and abolished slavery, fundamentally reshaping North American society and establishing the United States as an ascendant power.

North America became the dominant global economic and military superpower in the twentieth century, especially after World War II. Its technological innovation, resource wealth, and cultural influence shape world affairs.
